records.title: Show HN: Orisuji, a maze you solve by folding your phone
records.author: friggeri
records.storyText:
When Apple announced the iPhone Duo I felt the same excitement that I had felt when I got my first iPhone, way back when.

I remember playing Tap Tap Revenge, Fruit Ninja and all those other games that really took advantage of the new hardware to create new experiences. I also loved playing cute puzzles like Cut the Rope and Where’s my water.

A month ago, I got the itch to build something for the duo, in the lineage of those apps. Something that would be a fun puzzle with a unique game mechanic. I started with a simple premise: what if the cover screen was partly transparent? That could make a fun maze that you have to fold and unfold as you solve it.

Orisuji is a turn based paper maze, when the phone is open you have your base maze on the right part of the screen, but the only way to solve it is to figure out when to fold/unfold it to create bridges and new routes. Along the way you’ll encounter increasing complex levels: cats and foxes patrolling, doors you need to unlock, platforms you can toggle, and floors that crumble under you.

Some fun things I built/had to do that aren’t obvious:

- I built a web based level editor that runs the game’s rules engine compiled from Swift to wasm.

- Every level is validated by a solver that identifies shortest solutions, lints the board and identifies which “tricks” are required to solve it. This helped me a few times when designing levels where I would make a change but accidentally would introduce a shortcut.

- Figuring out how to translate the fold mechanic to non iPhone Duos was a cool challenge, I ended up adding a “virtual” on screen fold, which still doesn’t justice to the game.

- As much as I would love to have some data on how people play the game, it was super important to me that the game worked totally offline, not collecting any data.

It was so incredibly fun to build this, as you can expect I leaned heavily into agentic tools, which enabled me to move pretty fast. Every puzzled was however designed by hand, AIs are not good at “fun”, and from a game design perspective this was the most interesting part to me.

The whole game costs $4.99, all 69 levels (and already working on new worlds), no IAP ever.

Trailer: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w98lwzHgGWA

If you’ve got a duo (or not) I’d love to hear your feedback. And more than happy to answer anything about building/designing it!

records.title: Show HN: ReVault – new secure archive format
records.author: bsutto
records.storyText:
reVault is a new, secure-by-default archive format called a lockbox, designed to be simple to use.

I've been working on reVault for about 2 years. It was originally written in Dart, but with the improvements in AI, I decided to port it to Rust using AI.

It's now in beta, so I'm looking for feedback, particularly around the different language bindings.

A lockbox is encrypted, signed and compressed by default. Each can be disabled selectively.

  - Hybrid post-quantum or passphrase encryption, including metadata.
  - Zstd compression.
  - Pure Rust libraries wherever possible.
We intend to phase out remaining C code as alternatives become available. The project has been scanned using OpenAI's Daybreak cyber security tools.

The manual is a work in progress: https://docs.revault.onepub.dev/

reVault supports Linux, macOS and Windows, x64 and arm64, plus Wasm. The core is Rust, with bindings for C/C++, Java, Dart, Python, Ruby, JS/TypeScript, Go, C#, Kotlin, Lua, PHP and Swift.

Within a lockbox you can store:

  - Files, directories, permissions and symlinks.
  - Variables.
  - Forms.
Variables, forms and the lockbox itself can have descriptions.

reVault uses a portable vault (just another lockbox with structured content) to hold your keys, contacts' keys, lockbox aliases and form definitions.

It ties into your platform's secure store, so logging into your desktop unlocks your vault. You don't have to enter a passphrase every time you access a lockbox. You can disable this.

There are lots of shortcuts. Creating a lockbox stores an alias in your vault, based on its filename or a name you choose:

  lbx create /some/path/mybox.lbox
  lbx mybox open --duration 1h
  lbx mybox var set KEY VALUE
Set a default lockbox and you can leave its name out:

  lbx session default mybox
  lbx var get KEY
You can mirror a directory tree into a lockbox and update it when the directory changes:

  lbx store.lbox mirrors project create --from ./project --to /projects/project
  lbx store.lbox mirrors update
The API lets you read, write and seek within files without extracting them to the filesystem. Each lockbox has a table of contents, so extracting a single file from a multi-gigabyte lockbox is fast.

Recovery

Updates are transactional, with automatic rollback for failed updates. The format is designed for recovery: content is stored in pages, allowing unaffected content to be recovered if part of a lockbox is corrupted.

Sharing

An encrypted lockbox is more useful if you can share it.

reVault has an open-source keyserver for exchanging public keys, with validation through a second trusted channel. It's still experimental.

OnePub has donated a server to run a single keyserver. If you're interested in donating resources, I'd like to bring up a second redundant server. It's pure Rust, uses under 100 MB RSS and supports rate limits.

To publish your default profile's public key:

  lbx vault profiles email you@example.com
  lbx vault profiles publish
Give the publish code to your contact. They can import your key:

  lbx vault contacts receive <publish-code> <contact-name>
Display your profile's fingerprint and exchange it through a second trusted channel:

  lbx vault profiles fingerprint
Repeat the process in the opposite direction to get their key. Once you have it, grant them access to your default lockbox:

  lbx access grant alice
You can then email the encrypted lockbox to Alice.

To install the CLI and get started:

  cargo install revault_cli
  lbx vault init
  lbx completion install
Completion installation detects your shell. To diagnose issues:

  lbx doctor
The language bindings are published to their respective package repositories.

I'm looking for constructive criticism of the project on its own merits, particularly the APIs and language bindings. I'm not interested in a debate about using AI.

records.title: Show HN: Find overlapping Rust tests with mutation testing
records.author: yasuyuky
records.storyText:
To tackle the ever-increasing number of tests, I built cargo-test-prune.

The idea behind it is to use cargo-mutants to generate mutants, and then solve the set cover problem for those mutants to suggest which tests can be eliminated. (use a greedy algorithm to cover the detected mutants with fewer tests)

I came up with this as a countermeasure against the monotonically increasing tests that tend to accumulate, especially when coding with AI.

In fact, this very repository was also written using AI.

I ran this tool on a previous revision of this repository. There were 11 tests and 108 generated mutants: 73 were caught by the tests, 23 survived, and 12 failed to compile. I removed the 5 tests suggested by the tool and re-ran the same 108 mutants. The remaining 6 tests caught the exact same 73 mutants.

Tests partly serve as documentation, so simply applying this isn't necessarily recommended, but since writing less code still holds value in the AI era, I think this tool could be quite useful.

Three years ago, our dog was sideswiped by a car and my wife took him to the local vet in Berkeley. Unfortunately, things did not go well and to cut a long story short, he passed after 2 days and $13k of bills for very limited care. I was surprised to learn that the seemingly mom & pop practice had been acquired by a PE-owned consolidator and that around 50% of practices in the US are now owned by mostly PE-backed corporate groups - a trend that rapidly accelerated after COVID.

I started a small janky passion project called https://privateequityvet.org which used Leaflet.js to map corporately owned veterinary practices in the US. The site gradually took off, was covered on PBS Newshour and now gets 20k uniques a day.

A few months ago I launched IndependentVet.com which aims to be the opposite of the original site, helping pet parents in the US/Canada/UK identify locally owned veterinary practices. Just yesterday I launched native mobile apps that I developed over the course of three intense weeks of evenings and weekends using Opus 5.5. While it's early days, I'm really happy with how it turned out: https://independentvet.com/get

Would love to hear what you think!

records.title: Show HN: DeepSearch – Search engine built on DeepSeek API
records.author: try-working
records.storyText:
DeepSeek launched their search API so I had to build a search engine on top of it.

The search engine is very simple: add your DeepSeek API credentials or OAuth with your DeepSeek account and you can search the web using their API and view results in a familiar web interface.

Credentials are stored locally only.

The search engine exposes the operators from the API:

- Time

- Language

- Exact terms with "..." (like Google used to)

- Forbidden terms with "-"

- Site search and excluded sites

Search results expose things like domain authority, rank etc.

You can also switch to Ask and get a generated response for your question.

Give it a try and see if this works as a Google replacement. So far the results seem passable but I've only done quick test queries.

I also shared the source on GitHub so you could self-host or fork it into a local client.

The most interesting thing here would be to build a local client with history/memory, so that your knowledge compounds.

https://github.com/try-works/deepsearch

records.title: Show HN: A client-side adaptive cognitive test measuring micro-hesitations
records.author: mr-boombastic
records.storyText:
Hi HN! I’m not a software engineer by trade. My background is in behavioral science and human-computer interaction, but I wanted to solve a specific problem I found when applying for jobs which is the logical test. They are booooring, easy to cheat on if you really want to and provides very limited information about people. I built this prototype from scratch sing AI to bring my idea to life. So now I've been working on this side project for a Cognitive Adaption Engine (CAT/KAT in swedish) for about three weeks. Many pre-employment screening tests i've done use a static item bank and are very liberal with the time allowed on each question, making it easy for Vision LLMs or bots to beat. I wanted to see if I could build a fast, client-side engine (JS/SVG) that combats this problem by measuring certain biometric cognitive signatures like "switch cost" (how long it takes for your brain to re-adjust when logical rules change) and "post error-slowing". To go beyond the simple grading of correct/incorrect, this test dynamically gives you waves of patterns/challenges through a local item bank based on your millisecond response times. If you use an LLM, the constant latencies gets punished with a lower score. If they use a script, the complete lack of natural human variance will be picked up on. I am currently trying to calibrate a baseline and need high-aptitude users to stress-test it and to provide more data. It also makes it very fast to complete.

Everything runs 100% locally in your browser and since I did use AI, I would love your feedback on how the architecture holds up and the technical approach to anti-cheating or anything that comes to mind on this topic.

(Optional) When you finish the test, you can press Ctrl + Shift + X on the results page which unlocks a hidden admin console. There you can see more info on your performance and even download a HR-pdf that translate your data into three tailored interview questions. Unfortunately the admin page is in Swedish, but I believe you will get the idea.

records.author: Tomotsugu-dev
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I’m building Hindsight, a free, open-source activity tracker for Windows and macOS.

I know there are plenty of time trackers. I wanted something that combined automatic tracking, detailed charts, and cross-device sync in a lightweight app with an interface I enjoyed using. I couldn’t find a free option that fit, so I started building my own.

Hindsight records active apps and window titles while it’s running, without requiring you to start and stop timers. You can explore your activity through daily, weekly, and monthly charts, drill down into individual apps and window titles, and use a yearly heatmap to spot patterns. Categories are customizable.

There’s also an optional screenshot and OCR feature for finding something you previously saw on screen. Both are off by default. When enabled, you can search recognized text and jump back to the corresponding screenshot.

The AI features can generate daily summaries or answer questions about your activity, with links back to the underlying records so you can check the answers. You can use a local model or connect a cloud API; third-party API fees may apply.

Optional sync through Google Drive or WebDAV lets you view activity from Windows and Mac devices separately or together. I’ve also recently added plugin support so other developers can extend the app.

I’d appreciate feedback, particularly on how you’d want to explore your activity history. What would make this useful to you beyond simply showing how many hours you spent in each app?

Happy to answer questions about how it works.

records.title: Show HN: Reusable, spectraly shaped Blue Noise point clouds
records.author: adec314
records.storyText:
Blue noise is the task of sampling a collection of points optimally placed to cover space randomly yet uniformly.

-randomly: no periodic pattern or undesired ordered structure, to prevent aliasing effects.

-uniformly: no empty regions, clusters... that would unavoidably appear by just using a raw random generator because of natural fluctuations.

In spectral language, one can take the Fourier transform of the point cloud. For a blue noise, it's amplitude should be:

- 0 or small at low frequencies. This ensures long-range order.

- 1 or not too big at high frequencies (short-range disorder).

Hence blue noise: Imagine sending light on the point cloud; in some abstract sense, only the blue (high frequency) will pass through.

Many popular algorithms can sample blue noise: Poisson disks, void and clusters, Lloyd relaxation... but the bluest blue noise (those that show up as a hard 0-1 spectral step) comes from the most basic, brute-force algorithm you can imagine. Take points from a purely random generator, compare the Fourier transform with the 0-1 target, launch gradient descent... and wait. Wait because it has O(N^2) complexity. Well, it turns out in 2D / 3D, advanced fast Fourier techniques can bring it down to N log N, see https://github.com/martiniani-lab/FReSCo (not me), but this is limited to 2D / 3D point clouds.

So, all this just to say that I launched a high-quality but slow blue noise optimiser on the GPU, collected the samples in a reusable database and hope it could interest people from graphics, statistical physics, maybe also quasi-Monte Carlo integration (but this one is just a maybe, simple Sobol sequences are better than blue noise on many tasks) or just curious hackers.

Sampled clouds, all open access: 2D to 32D 1k to 130k points (and up to 30 millions in 2D / 3D thanks to the mentioned fast Fourier speed-up).

records.title: Show HN: Music player for visually exploring music collection
records.author: CP1979
records.storyText:
I created Melodex for rediscovering my music collection. I got bored of listening to the same songs over and over. Shuffle didn't do it for me either, as I wanted something that moved between the songs like a journey with more cohesion.

Alongside the ability to plan routes from a starting song to a final destination, the routes through the music map are navigable too.

There's a few other features like plugins to connect radio stations, or other music sources too which were a big project in terms of getting the plugin structure right to get working with almost any online source now.

Looking for feedback on the music map, how it can be further improved, how intuitive, did it lead to new musical discoveries of your music?

records.title: Show HN: Sparse kernel delivering 36% higher training throughput
records.author: jakcwi
records.storyText:
I developed a custom GPU kernel in Triton to accelerate training with a sparse feed-forward network (FFN).

With K=256, activating 256 of 4,096 FFN neurons per token (6.25%), the sparse model achieved 36% higher training throughput than its dense counterpart.

The kernel has so far been tested on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU and requires GPU hardware with BF16 support.

Whether a model trained with a sparse FFN and densified afterwards can match the quality of a model trained densely remains an open question. These early results have motivated me to continue training a larger model using this approach.

More about EUGEN and my work: https://jakubcwirlej.com/ai-dev/

records.title: Show HN: Claude Code(and others) embedded in your app
records.author: fullstackwife
records.storyText:
I started this project in 2024 when I got fascinated with LLMs, and what I did was a coding agent (CLI -> interactive -> GUI). I also added an integration with Vite for having it embedded inside my apps(mostly games). Few months ago I pivoted it to become a low profile AI provider wrapper library (think jQuery for LLM usage), because I realized there is no point to have custom coding agent.

Recently I did yet another pivot, and now it is a solution that allows you to embed Claude Code inside of your app, and use it directly from there for 1. development, 2. every day ops and automate the tasks in the app

In theory all you need to try it is this command: `npx genaicode embed`, I wonder if anyone would like to give it a try, and let me know how it worked!

records.title: Show HN: Loböle, open-source parametric CAD that AI agents can drive
records.author: eliasaronson
records.storyText:
I could never get used to FreeCAD, so I built my own. It turns out Claude is really good at using it.

Loböle is a parametric B-Rep CAD built on OpenCASCADE and Vulkan, with sketches, assemblies, drawings, FEM and CAM.

The GUI, Python scripts and AI agents all go through the same commands, so an agent can do anything you can in the GUI. The engine, watch and bicycle in the README were each built by Claude writing a script against it.
